arab-conquest-of-egypt.name: Arab conquest of Egypt
arab-conquest-of-egypt.summary: The Rashidun Caliphate's conquest of Byzantine Egypt between 639 and 642 AD, ending nearly a thousand years of Greco-Roman rule there.

roda-island.name: Roda Island
roda-island.summary: Island neighbourhood on the Nile in central Cairo, also known as Manial al-Roda, part of the Old Cairo district.

al-mutawakkil.name: al-Mutawakkil
al-mutawakkil.summary: Tenth Abbasid caliph, ruling from 847 until his assassination in 861, remembered as devoutly religious and a prolific builder whose caliphate reached its greatest territorial extent.

al-farghani.name: Al-Farghani
al-farghani.summary: Ninth-century astronomer at the Abbasid court in Baghdad known for a widely used summary of Ptolemy's Almagest, who also oversaw construction projects on rivers in Cairo, Egypt.

fustat.name: Fustat
fustat.summary: The first capital of Egypt under Muslim rule, founded in 641 near present-day Cairo; it peaked at about 200,000 people in the 12th century before being burned in 1168 to keep it from Crusader hands.

al-maqrizi.name: Al-Maqrizi
al-maqrizi.summary: A medieval Egyptian historian and biographer (1364-1442) of the Mamluk era, regarded as the most influential historian of premodern Egypt.

mulukhiyah.name: Mulukhiyah
mulukhiyah.summary: A traditional Egyptian and Arab dish made from the leaves of a jute plant, cooked into a thick, mucilaginous broth or stew and usually served with rice.

mu-awiya-i.name: Mu'awiya I
mu-awiya-i.summary: Founder and first caliph of the Umayyad Caliphate, ruling from 661 to 680; a late convert to Islam who rose through the early caliphates before contesting Ali for power.

makuria.name: Makuria
makuria.summary: Medieval Nubian kingdom, capital Dongola, in what is now northern Sudan and southern Egypt; it repelled an Arab invasion in 652 and kept a resulting peace treaty for six centuries.

banganarti.name: Banganarti
banganarti.summary: A small village in Sudan near Old Dongola, site of an important medieval Christian pilgrimage center and the remains of a substantial church.

abbasid-architecture.name: Abbasid architecture
abbasid-architecture.summary: The architectural style developed under the Abbasid Caliphate (750-1258), centered in Iraq, blending Mesopotamian and Persian influences and spreading across the Islamic world.

dongola-reach.name: Dongola Reach
dongola-reach.summary: A roughly 160 km stretch of the Nile in Upper Nubia, Sudan, between the Third and Fourth Cataracts, that formed the historic heartland of ancient Nubia.

alodia.name: Alodia
alodia.summary: Medieval Christian kingdom in what is now central Sudan, with its capital at Soba, that thrived as a multicultural trading hub roughly from the 6th century until around 1500.

fatimid-caliphate.name: Fatimid Caliphate
fatimid-caliphate.summary: An Isma'ili Shia caliphate ruling North Africa and West Asia from the 10th to 12th centuries CE, claiming descent from Muhammad's daughter Fatima, with Egypt as its eventual centre.

fatimid-architecture.name: Fatimid architecture
fatimid-architecture.summary: The building style of the Fatimid Caliphate (909–1171), blending Abbasid, Byzantine and Coptic influences, seen mainly in surviving mosques and gates of Cairo.

old-dongola.name: Old Dongola
old-dongola.summary: A now-deserted Nubian town on the Nile in Sudan, capital of the medieval kingdom of Makuria from the 4th to 14th century, later replaced by modern Dongola downstream.

rashidun-caliphate.name: Rashidun Caliphate
rashidun-caliphate.summary: Early Islamic state (632–661 CE) led by the first four caliphs after Muhammad's death, which rapidly expanded into the dominant power of West Asia and North Africa.

baqt.name: Baqt
baqt.summary: A 7th-century treaty between the Christian Nubian kingdom of Makuria and the Muslim rulers of Egypt, reputedly the longest-lasting treaty in history, lasting nearly 700 years.

abd-allah-ibn-sa-d.name: Abdallah ibn Sa'd
abd-allah-ibn-sa-d.summary: An Arab administrator, scribe and military commander and early convert to Islam who governed Upper Egypt under caliph Uthman and co-founded the Islamic navy that seized Cyprus and defeated a Byzantine fleet.

amr-ibn-al-as.name: Amr ibn al-As
amr-ibn-al-as.summary: Arab commander and companion of Muhammad who led the Muslim conquest of Egypt and served as its governor in 640–646 and 658–664, founding Fustat as its capital.

john-the-deacon-egyptian-chronicler.name: John the Deacon
john-the-deacon-egyptian-chronicler.summary: Coptic Orthodox chronicler (writing c. 768–770) whose Life of the Patriarch Michael is the main source for Christian Nubia in the early 8th century, though not always reliable.

mangonel.name: Mangonel
mangonel.summary: A rope-pulled siege weapon, also called the traction trebuchet, used in China from the Warring States period and across Eurasia by the 6th century AD, later replaced by the counterweight trebuchet.

muhammad-ibn-abi-bakr.name: Muhammad ibn Abi Bakr
muhammad-ibn-abi-bakr.summary: Arab commander and loyal supporter of the fourth caliph Ali who served as governor of Egypt from 657 before being defeated, captured, and executed in 658.

ali.name: Ali
ali.summary: Cousin and son-in-law of the prophet Muhammad, the first Shia Imam and fourth Rashidun caliph, who served from 656 until his assassination in 661.

mu-awiya-ibn-hudayj.name: Mu'awiya ibn Hudayj
mu-awiya-ibn-hudayj.summary: A general of the Kinda tribe who served under Caliph Mu'awiya I, fighting in the early Muslim conquests in Syria, Sicily and Ifriqiya, and against the Sasanids.

ibn-abd-al-hakam.name: Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam
ibn-abd-al-hakam.summary: A 9th-century Sunni historian and jurist from Fustat, Egypt, whose account of the conquest of Egypt, North Africa and al-Andalus is among the earliest surviving Arabic-language histories.

ibn-a-tham-al-kufi.name: Ahmad al-Kufi
ibn-a-tham-al-kufi.summary: A 9th-century Shia Arab historian and poet whose 'Book of Conquests' survives in a single two-volume manuscript.

alexander-romance.name: Coptic Alexander Romance
alexander-romance.summary: A fantastical, legend-filled account of Alexander the Great's life, originally written in Greek before 338 AD and translated into dozens of languages across Europe, Asia and Africa.

white-monastery.name: White Monastery
white-monastery.summary: A Coptic Orthodox monastery near Sohag in Upper Egypt named for Saint Shenoute, once home to one of the largest Coptic libraries known.

alexander-the-great.name: Alexander the Great
alexander-the-great.summary: King of Macedon from 336 BC who conquered much of the known world by age 30, creating an empire stretching from Greece to India; tutored by Aristotle.

old-nubian.name: Old Nubian
old-nubian.summary: An extinct Nubian language used across the kingdom of Makuria from the 8th to 15th century, preserved in religious and administrative texts written in a Coptic-derived alphabet.

coptic-language.name: Coptic language
coptic-language.summary: The last stage of the Egyptian language, spoken from the 3rd century AD and written in the Coptic alphabet; replaced by Arabic but still used in church liturgy.

asyut.name: Asyut
asyut.summary: City in Upper Egypt and capital of the modern Asyut Governorate, home to one of the largest Coptic Christian communities in the country.

oxyrhynchus.name: Oxyrhynchus
oxyrhynchus.summary: A city in Middle Egypt, also called Al-Bahnasa, whose archaeological site has yielded an enormous collection of papyrus texts from the Ptolemaic and Roman periods.

bohairic-coptic.name: Bohairic Coptic
bohairic-coptic.summary: A dialect of the Coptic Egyptian language attested from the 8th century CE, which became the chief liturgical language of the Coptic Orthodox Church.

coptic-script.name: Coptic script
coptic-script.summary: The writing system used for the Coptic language, based on the Greek alphabet with extra letters borrowed from Egyptian Demotic script, the first alphabetic script for Egyptian.

meroitic-script.name: Meroitic script
meroitic-script.summary: Two related scripts, cursive and hieroglyphic, developed to write the Meroitic language of the Kingdom of Kush from the 3rd century BC, used into the 5th century AD.

kingdom-of-kush.name: Kingdom of Kush
kingdom-of-kush.summary: An ancient kingdom in Nubia along the Nile in what is now Sudan and Egypt, rising from the city-state of Kerma and later ruling Egypt itself in the 8th century BCE under King Piye.

pope-benjamin-i-of-alexandria.name: Benjamin I of Alexandria
pope-benjamin-i-of-alexandria.summary: 38th Pope of Alexandria, regarded as one of the greatest Coptic patriarchs, who led the church through Sasanian conquest, Byzantine reconquest, and the Arab conquest of 642.

pope-agatho-of-alexandria.name: Agathon
pope-agatho-of-alexandria.summary: The 39th Pope of Alexandria and Patriarch of the Coptic Church, who led it during persecution by a Byzantine patriarch and chose his successor from a dream.

samuel-the-confessor.name: Samuel of Qalamun
samuel-the-confessor.summary: Coptic Orthodox saint (597–695), also known as Samuel the Confessor, remembered for enduring torture under Byzantine rule and for the monastery he built at Mount Qalamoun.

john-of-niki.name: John of Nikiû
john-of-niki.summary: Egyptian Coptic bishop of Nikiû (fl. 680–690) who administered Upper Egypt's monasteries and wrote a Chronicle from Adam to the Muslim conquest of Egypt, preserving unique historical details.

koine-greek.name: Koine Greek
koine-greek.summary: The common form of Greek spoken and written across the Hellenistic world, Roman Empire and early Byzantine Empire, spreading after Alexander the Great's conquests and used for the Septuagint and New Testament.

al-aswani.name: Al-Aswani
al-aswani.summary: Tenth-century Egyptian diplomat and Fatimid missionary sent to Nubia, whose account is the only surviving eyewitness description of medieval Nubia besides a brief one by Ibn Hawqal.

musawwarat-es-sufra.name: Musawwarat es-Sufra
musawwarat-es-sufra.summary: Large Meroitic temple complex in Sudan dating to the 3rd century BC, notable for its many representations of elephants and now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

soba-city.name: Soba
soba-city.summary: An archaeological site in central Sudan that was capital of the medieval Christian kingdom of Alodia from the 6th century until around 1500.

severus-ibn-al-muqaffa.name: Severus ibn al-Muqaffa
severus-ibn-al-muqaffa.summary: Egyptian Coptic Orthodox bishop, author and historian who died in 987, serving as bishop of Hermopolis Magna in Upper Egypt under Fatimid rule.

al-maqdisi.name: Al-Maqdisi
al-maqdisi.summary: A medieval Arab geographer, author of a major work describing the regions of the Islamic world, praised for his vivid descriptions especially of his native Palestine.

coptic-calendar.name: Coptic calendar
coptic-calendar.summary: A liturgical calendar used in Egypt, kept for fiscal purposes until 1875, with a leap year every four years without exception, unlike the Gregorian calendar.

ahmad-ibn-tulun.name: Ahmad ibn Tulun
ahmad-ibn-tulun.summary: Founder of the Tulunid dynasty that ruled Egypt and Syria from 868 to 905, who built an independent administration and military and constructed a new capital, al-Qata'i.

samarra.name: Samarra
samarra.summary: A city on the Tigris in Iraq, founded in 836 CE by the Abbasid caliph al-Mu'tasim as a new capital and military base; its ruins are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

astrolabe.name: Astrolabe
astrolabe.summary: An ancient astronomical instrument and star chart used to measure the altitude of celestial bodies and to determine time, latitude, or position.

al-balaw.name: Al-Balawi
al-balaw.summary: Tenth-century Egyptian Arab historian from the tribe of Bali, a branch of Quda'a.

mosque-of-ibn-tulun.name: Mosque of Ibn Tulun
mosque-of-ibn-tulun.summary: Mosque in Cairo built 876–879, the oldest well-preserved mosque in Egypt, its design inspired by Abbasid mosques of Samarra in Iraq.

hyksos.name: Hyksos
hyksos.summary: Kings of Egypt's Fifteenth Dynasty, about 1650 to 1550 BCE, likely of Levantine origin, who were the first foreign rulers of Egypt.

roman-egypt.name: Aegyptus
roman-egypt.summary: Roman imperial province covering most of Egypt from 30 BC to AD 642, a major grain producer and the wealthiest province outside Italy, with Alexandria as its capital.

justinian-i.name: Justinian I
justinian-i.summary: Roman emperor from 527 to 565 whose generals reconquered much of the former Western Roman Empire and who is remembered for his sweeping rewrite of Roman law.

theodora-wife-of-justinian-i.name: Theodora
theodora-wife-of-justinian-i.summary: Eastern Roman empress (c. 490/500–548) and wife of Justinian I, a former actress of humble birth who became a key political adviser and helped suppress the Nika riots of 532.

dyophysitism.name: Dyophysitism
dyophysitism.summary: The Christian doctrine that Jesus Christ has two distinct natures, divine and human, held by most denominations but rejected by Oriental Orthodox churches, which favor Miaphysitism instead.

miaphysitism.name: Miaphysitism
miaphysitism.summary: A Christian doctrine holding that Jesus is fully divine and fully human in a single nature, held by the Oriental Orthodox Churches in contrast to the two-nature view set at Chalcedon in 451.

blemmyes.name: Blemmyes
blemmyes.summary: An Eastern Desert people recorded from the 7th century BCE to the 8th century CE, who by the late 4th century had occupied Lower Nubia and founded a kingdom there.

narses.name: Narses
narses.summary: A Roman general and statesman of Armenian heritage (c. 478–573) who helped reconquer Italy for Emperor Justinian I, defeating the Ostrogoths at Taginae in 552 and Mons Lactarius in 553.

philae-temple-complex.name: Philae
philae-temple-complex.summary: An island-based temple complex on the Nile near Aswan, Egypt, dismantled and relocated in the 1960s–70s to save it from flooding by the new Aswan Dam.

justin-i.name: Justin I
justin-i.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 518 to 527, a former peasant and soldier who rose through the army to the throne in his late 60s and founded the Justinian dynasty.

mamluk.name: Mamluks
mamluk.summary: Non-Arab enslaved soldiers, often of Turkic or Circassian origin, who converted to Islam and trained for war before being freed to serve as an elite military and political class in Egypt for nearly 1,000 years.

tulunids.name: Tulunids
tulunids.summary: A dynasty of Turkic origin that ruled Egypt on behalf of the Abbasid Caliphate, autonomous from 868 until 905, founded by the officer Ahmad ibn Tulun.

ikhshidid-dynasty.name: Ikhshidid dynasty
ikhshidid-dynasty.summary: A dynasty of Turkic Mamluk governors who ruled Egypt and parts of the Levant from 935 to 969 on behalf of the Abbasid Caliphate, ending when the Fatimids conquered Fustat.

justin-ii.name: Justin II
justin-ii.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 565 to 578, nephew of Justinian I, whose harder line toward neighboring powers revived war with Persia and began the Byzantine-Lombard wars.

tiberius-ii-constantine.name: Tiberius II Constantine
tiberius-ii-constantine.summary: Eastern Roman emperor from 578 to 582, whose reign saw warfare with Persia and Avar incursions into the empire.

malik-al-ashtar.name: Malik al-Ashtar
malik-al-ashtar.summary: Arab military commander and loyal general of Caliph Ali who fought at the battles of the Camel and Siffin, poisoned in 658 en route to govern Egypt.

nusaybin.name: Nisibis
nusaybin.summary: An ancient city in northern Mesopotamia held in turn by Assyrians, Persians, Seleucids, Romans and Sasanians, and made capital of Roman Mesopotamia after a treaty in 298 CE.

marwan-ii.name: Marwan II
marwan-ii.summary: Fourteenth and last caliph of the Umayyad Caliphate (ruled 744–750), whose reign was dominated by civil war and ended when the Abbasid Revolution toppled the dynasty.

kyriakos-of-makuria.name: Kyriakos
kyriakos-of-makuria.summary: King of Makuria, a Christian kingdom in Nubia, active around the mid-8th century.

council-of-chalcedon.name: Council of Chalcedon
council-of-chalcedon.summary: The fourth ecumenical council of the Christian Church, held in 451 CE, which declared Jesus fully divine and fully human, rejecting rival views that saw him as only divine or as having separate natures.

pope-of-the-coptic-orthodox-church.name: Pope of Alexandria (Coptic Pope)
pope-of-the-coptic-orthodox-church.summary: Leader of the Coptic Orthodox Church, traditionally the successor to Saint Mark as bishop of Alexandria; the seat has been based in Cairo since 1047.
pope-of-the-coptic-orthodox-church.source_title: Pope of the Coptic Orthodox Church

al-azhar-university.name: Al-Azhar University
al-azhar-university.summary: Founded in Cairo in 970 by the Fatimid Caliphate, it is Egypt's oldest university and one of the most prestigious centers of Islamic learning in the world.

mark-the-evangelist.name: Mark the Evangelist
mark-the-evangelist.summary: Early Christian traditionally credited as author of the Gospel of Mark and founder of the episcopal see of Alexandria; venerated as a saint with a feast day on April 25.

egyptian-arabic.name: Egyptian Arabic (Masri)
egyptian-arabic.summary: Colloquial Arabic dialect spoken by Egyptians, the most widely spoken and studied vernacular form of Arabic thanks to Egypt's cultural influence.

coptic-orthodox-church.name: Coptic Orthodox Church
coptic-orthodox-church.summary: An Oriental Orthodox Christian church based in Egypt, traditionally founded by Saint Mark around AD 42, and the largest Christian group in Egypt and the Middle East.
